title: Prostate cancer can be diagnosed without invasive biopsy
author: Michael Searles
content:
Prostate cancer can be diagnosed without an invasive biopsy, a study has found.
Experts from University College London Hospitals (UCLH) said some men could have the disease detected through an MRI scan alone and not need procedures that carry a high risk of side effects.
Currently, NHS hospitals either give men with suspected prostate cancer an MRI, with doctors then deciding whether to take a biopsy, or they take a biopsy straight away.
But a study of 880 men found that using MRI scans and blood tests, as well as getting an expert opinion, detected the disease 99 per cent of the time.
Biopsies involve a small needle being put into the prostate to take a tissue sample.
There are two types of biopsy for prostate cancer, with needles inserted in different places. Both come with the risk of side effects, cancers being missed and the detection of cancers that may never need treating.
This is one of the reasons why health officials have not approved a wider screening using prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood tests, because people whose results reveal suspected cancer have historically gone on to have biopsies.
But the new study found that some men could have their cancer diagnosed by MRI alone.
The findings could reignite calls for a screening programme.
The Telegraph has been campaigning for the rollout of targeted screening for thousands more men at increased risk, including black men and those with a family history of the disease.
Last week, this newspaper revealed that men aged over 50 are no longer entitled to a blood test to help identify the disease, with GPs deciding who receives one.
summary: A study of 880 men by experts at University College London Hospitals found that prostate cancer can be diagnosed using MRI scans, blood tests, and expert opinion without the need for an invasive biopsy. The findings show this non-invasive approach detected the disease 99 percent of the time, potentially avoiding the risks of side effects associated with tissue samples. This discovery could reignite calls for a wider targeted screening programme for prostate cancer.
key_points: A study of 880 men showed prostate cancer can be diagnosed through MRI scans and blood tests without an invasive biopsy.
The non-invasive method detected the disease 99 percent of the time.
Biopsies carry risks of side effects, missed cancers, and detection of harmless cancers.
The findings could reignite calls for wider targeted screening programmes for men at increased risk.

title: Deaf patient given wrong jab due to sign language error, report says
author: Beth Rose; Emma Tracey
content:
![Close-up of a person receiving an injection in the upper arm, with a healthcare worker holding a syringe and supporting the arm. The image focuses on the vaccination procedure in a clinical setting, with the background softly blurred.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/a8a3/live/e8eb51e0-9b24-11f1-9a2c-6d6ac3827d20.jpg)
- Published
A deaf woman was given the wrong vaccine because she was not provided with a British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter at her doctor's surgery, a report says.
The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) said disabled people were being let down by inaccessible communications.
It said the patient, Samantha, had booked a flu jab but was instead given a Covid vaccine after staff failed to show her a BSL video which would have highlighted the error. She said the experience had had a "profound impact" on her.
The Department of Health and Social Care said the "deeply upsetting stories" were "completely unacceptable" and NHS and social care organisations had a duty to make services accessible.
The PHSO investigates complaints about UK government departments, public organisations and the NHS in England.
It said public services were legally required to support people with their accessible communication needs, which might be due to a disability, neurodivergence or English not being their first language.
Samantha had booked her flu and Covid jabs for separate weeks and showed a nurse a note on her phone which said she was there for the "flu jab only", the PHSO said.
Despite that, the practice said it believed it had correctly established Samantha wanted the Covid vaccine and had got her consent through her grandmother, even though she had early-stage dementia and was not in the treatment room.
Following an investigation, the PHSO recommended the surgery should apologise and pay Samantha Â£450. It has also since signed a contract with a sign language interpreting company.
The NHS Northamptonshire Integrated Care Board said it was "very sorry" about Samantha's experience, and that it expected practices to make "reasonable adjustments to support effective communication".
The PHSO said it had found disabled people risked not getting vital information about their healthcare, finances or employment because of a lack of accessible formats such as large print or audio materials.
Since April 2020, it said it had concluded 623 investigations related to reasonable adjustments, of which 496 were upheld or partly upheld.
The report also highlighted the case of Alan Graham, who was deaf and was being treated for heart failure at University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Trust.
When an interpreter was not available, hospital staff asked his teenage grandson to interpret for the family and tell Graham's deaf daughter that he might die.
![Alan Graham pictured holding a fish. He is wearing a khaki hat and fisherman's jacket. He has a grey beard and wears circular silver framed glasses](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/062f/live/0a9fb2e0-9b16-11f1-b792-a710e56a11dc.jpg)
Alan Graham was being treated for cancer in Birmingham when his grandson was asked to interpret serious news to the family
Following an ombudsman investigation, the trust apologised and said "we did not get things right".
They said new measures had been introduced to help deaf patients, including strengthening awareness and accessibility arrangements to ensure patients' communication needs were better met.
"We remain committed to learning from this and to providing inclusive, compassionate care for all our patients," they said.
Following the report by the ombudsman, NHS England said it was "completely unacceptable for those who are deaf or have visual loss to face barriers to accessing or understanding the healthcare they need".
It added it had recently refreshed its standards setting out how services should provide safe and effective care for those with communication needs.
The PHSO said that while it was not a regulator, it could order public organisations to pay financial compensation if it upheld a complaint.
Rebecca Hilsenrath, its chief executive, said: "When people feel they are not listened to and that their needs are not met, they lose trust in the very services designed to support them."
In its report, the PHSO highlighted North Cheshire and Mersey NHS Foundation Trust as a good example of providing effective communication, after it worked with local advocacy groups and deaf people to improve its service for deaf patients who reported feeling excluded.
The trust has provided guides for patients on how to access interpreting and translation services, increasing the use of interpreters by 50% in one year.
summary: A Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman report revealed that a deaf woman named Samantha was given the wrong vaccine after being denied a British Sign Language interpreter at her surgery. The report highlighted multiple cases where disabled patients faced inaccessible communications, including a hospital asking a teenager to interpret his grandfather's critical medical news. The ombudsman recommended apologies and compensation in the investigated cases, prompting calls from health authorities for better accessibility and reasonable adjustments.
key_points: A deaf patient booked a flu jab but received a Covid vaccine instead due to a lack of a BSL interpreter.
The PHSO report found disabled people are frequently let down by inaccessible communications in public services.
In another highlighted case, a deaf patient's teenage grandson was asked to interpret critical end-of-life information.
The surgery involved in Samantha's case was recommended to apologize and pay £450, and has since hired a sign language interpreting company.
NHS England stated that communication barriers are unacceptable and noted that standards for accessible care have been refreshed.

title: Shropshire farmers scared about shortage in bluetongue vaccine
author: Charlie Stubbs
content:
![There is a man in a dark green polo shirt, with 'NFU' in yellow letters next to it. He has grey thin hair and is standing. To his left, there is his buggy, which is gret and has a window. To his right, there are cows.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/3803/live/1e89b160-9b08-11f1-b792-a710e56a11dc.jpg)
Richard Yates originally only vaccinated his cows against bluetongue but when cases were reported nationally, he also did his sheep
- Published
A farmer in Shropshire says he is worried for animals across the country because of the spread of an outbreak of the potentially fatal bluetongue virus amid a vaccine shortage.
Richard Yates, from Middleton Scriven near Bridgnorth, at first only vaccinated his cattle, but once cases started to rise in the South West, he jabbed his sheep.
It is now "extremely difficult to get the vaccine", he said and warned farmers could be faced with "considerable losses" if their animals died from the outbreak,.
The Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was "working closely with the industry and is putting processes in for additional vaccine supplies".
Bluetongue is an insect-borne viral disease affecting sheep and cattle among other animals, mainly spread by biting midges, which thrive in long, hot summers like the one the UK is experiencing.
There are currently 456 cases in the UK, external, none in Shropshire, but that number is expected to rise across the country.
The UK's chief veterinary officer committed earlier this month to "ramp up" testing and wanted all farmers to get the vaccine when it became available.
![There is a herd of sheep in a field of brown grass and waste. There is around 50 and they have white and black heads and wool coats the same colour as the grass.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/1539/live/23f41b40-9b08-11f1-b792-a710e56a11dc.jpg)
Yates got his sheep vaccinated before the vaccine shortage
Yates said the virus was a big issue in Belgium and the Netherlands two years ago and killed cattle and sheep there "in their droves".
"[Animals] can be healthy one day and dead the next," he added.
"It can also cause abortions, stillbirths, reducing fertility. It is devastating."
Yates said the vaccinations he gave his animals last year could still give them some protection.
"There will be some benefit if the animals are vaccinated last year [as it is] kicking around in their system," he said.
"But it evolves and mutates. Twenty-five years ago, there was a different strain of bluetongue.
"I remember going to the old Royal Show and that was the next big problem that was coming our way. We all vaccinated and after a year it disappeared."
'Worst outbreak'
Vets across the county have encouraged farmers to take up the vaccine by going on to a waiting list.
The shortage was because of issues with supply and demand because of "unprecedented levels" of need, according to Susan Carr, a farm vet at Severn Edge Practice in Bridgnorth.
"There is about 20,000 doses on our waiting list but I can imagine other practices are going through the same," she added.
"We are importing a lot of stock at the minute from Europe; it is a UK-licensed vaccine but there just isn't the stock in Europe.
"It's just taking time and obviously at the minute that's not what people want to hear."
Carr has worked as a vet for 12 years and said, about this outbreak, she had never seen it so bad.
"This is the worst notifiable disease outbreak I have had to deal with," she added.
"The only other [outbreak] we have had was bird flu a few years back."
"[It was] pretty bad around here and some of us did go and work alongside the ministry there with outbreaks but this has by far been sadly the the most the biggest one I've seen."
The spokesperson for Defra said they recognised how concerning bluetongue was for farmers and urged them and vets to place vaccine orders.
"There is a wide range of support available to help farmers protect their livestock and we will continue to monitor the situation closely," they added.
summary: Shropshire farmers and veterinarians are expressing deep concern over a vaccine shortage as the insect-borne bluetongue virus spreads across the UK, threatening livestock with death and reduced fertility. Farmer Richard Yates warned that animals could face considerable losses, while local vets report unprecedented demand with thousands of doses currently on waiting lists. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) stated it is working closely with the industry to secure additional vaccine supplies.
key_points: A shortage of the bluetongue vaccine has made it extremely difficult for farmers to protect their sheep and cattle.
There are currently 456 cases of the potentially fatal, insect-borne virus in the UK, with numbers expected to rise.
Local vets report unprecedented demand, with a single practice in Bridgnorth holding a waiting list for about 20,000 doses.
Defra stated it is working with the industry and putting processes in place for additional vaccine supplies.

title: UK salmonella outbreak leaves one dead and more than 200 ill
author: Chris Baraniuk
content:
- Chris Baraniuk
- Belfast
One person has died and 207 have become ill in a UK outbreak of salmonella, health authorities have said.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has launched an investigation into the recent spike in confirmed cases, most of which have occurred since the beginning of July.1 The contamination is genetically linked to a previous outbreak last year, which was traced to imported eggs.
Almost all cases (199) in the current outbreak were reported in England, and the two regions worst affected are Yorkshire …

Most of the cases have been reported since the beginning of July.
The contamination is genetically linked to a previous outbreak last year involving imported eggs.
Almost all of the cases, numbering 199, were reported in England.

title: Bowel cancer cases in under-50s at record high in Scotland
author: Aimee Stanton; Susie Forrest
content:
![Anona Gauld is wearing a pink and black spotty shirt and black glasses. She is smiling and there is a 40th birthday cake in front of her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/0751/live/be585630-9ae3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
Anona Gauld had just turned 40 when she was diagnosed with cancer
- Published
The number of people under the age of 50 being diagnosed with bowel cancer in Scotland has reached a record high, with almost 290 new cases in 2024, new figures show.
Bowel cancer is the fourth most common cancer in Scotland and is more often diagnosed in older people, with those over 50 offered screening in an attempt to detect it early.
However, new figures from Public Health Scotland, external show incidence has jumped by 38% in the under-50s over the past decade, with rates among younger women increasing by 56% in comparison with 24% in younger men.
Last month, the Scottish government asked the UK National screening committee to look at lowering the age for bowel screening to 45, to target younger patients.
Anona Gauld is one of a growing number of women under 50 being diagnosed with colorectal cancer, the medical name for bowel cancers.
She told the BBC her journey towards diagnosis started when she turned 40 in March 2023 and couldn't manage a birthday glass of fizz.
She'd had a mysterious pain in her shoulder for several weeks, which got worse every time she drank alcohol.
Gauld, from Stonehaven, thought she'd pulled a muscle or had been lying awkwardly in bed but by August she had been diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer, which had spread to her liver.
![Anona Gauld is wearing a white shirt and black glasses. She has mid length brown hair and is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/422a/live/d22e2810-9ae3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
Anona Gauld was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer
She had been going back and forth to her GP over several months but believes cancer wasn't initially considered, partly because of her age.
"One doctor even told me it was because my bra was too tight," she said.
"It was just a mystery."
Doctors later said the pain in her shoulder was actually coming from her liver, where they discovered a 13cm (5in) secondary tumour which had spread from her bowel.
![Lathan is sat in the driver's seat of the car and is smiling at the cancer. Anona is sat next to him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/960/cpsprodpb/8857/live/cce81140-9af2-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Anona has three children aged between 15 and 21
"It was a big shock," Gauld says.
"I was young, I was healthy. I had a healthy diet and you don't think it's going to happen to you."
She had chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and then surgery on her liver and bowel in 2024.
Last year the cancer came back in her liver, and since then she's been back on treatment.
"People can have stage 4 cancer and live for many years," she says.
"It is scary, because I've never asked my oncologist for any timeline or anything like that, because I don't want to know.
"I think it's just a case of living your life."
What is causing the rise in bowel cancer?
PHS said no definitive cause had been identified for the increase in bowel cancer in people aged under 50 and different potential causes were being investigated.
However, research suggests six in 10 colorectal cancers might be prevented, external through reducing weight, lowering consumption of red and processed meat, increasing dietary fibre and cutting down on alcohol.
Richard Wilson, professor of gastro-intestinal oncology at the University of Glasgow, told BBC Scotland the causes among the under-50s may be different compared with older patients, because of new risk factors that emerged after the 1990s.
"Ultra processed foods, we think, are the huge driver, because their use across all age groups has really increased," he said.
Wilson added that exposure to pesticides as well as micro and nanoplastics might also be factors.
"These tiny broken-down bits of plastic are in the air, in the water, in our food, and we're really concerned about that," he said.
"And then forever chemicals from non-stick frying pans, all of these affect the microbiome in the gut. That's the common denominator.
"We think all these things disrupt the healthy microbiome, cause inflammation, and might predispose to cancer."
Every year thousands of people across Scotland are diagnosed with bowel cancer.
In 2024, 4,275 cases were recorded - slightly down on 2023's figure of 4,395.
NHS inform, external lists the following as potential symptoms of bowel cancer:
- blood in your poo (stools)
- bleeding from your bottom
- a recent change in your poo, particularly looser poo or pooing more regularly
- new pain in your abdomen (tummy) that won't go away
- you've recently lost weight without trying
- more pale and tired than usual
Bowel screening is currently offered to people in Scotland, external aged 50 to 74 years old every two years - this is the same for people in England, external and Wales, external. In Northern Ireland, external screening is offered to people aged 60 to 74 every two years.
A spokesperson for the Scottish government said: "The Scottish government recognises that bowel cancers are occurring at higher rates that previously in people under the age of 50 and have submitted a proposal to the UK National screening committee review bowel screening eligibility to consider offering this to younger age groups."
However, Bowel Cancer UK chief executive Genevieve Edwards said any changes to Scotland's screening programme must be based on "robust evidence" and be supported by the NHS having the capacity to deliver them safely and effectively.
She said the rise in cases among people under 50 showed the need for further research and greater awareness.
"Scotland's focus must stay on diagnosing bowel cancer earlier and ensuring that everyone receives the right care at the right time," Edwards said.
Trends in other cancers
Bowel remains one of the most common cancer types in Scotland, alongside prostate, breast and lung - these cancers account for more than half (55%) of all diagnoses.
In men, a record number of men were diagnosed with prostate cancer in Scotland in 2024, the same year Sir Chris Hoy revealed he was being treated for the disease, with the number of diagnoses increasing by 6% compared to the year before.
Malignant melanoma of the skin (skin cancer) has also increased in men, rising by 28%.
However, there were also significant decreases in the rates of lung cancer, head and neck cancer, bladder cancer, oesophageal cancer and cancer of unknown primary in men.
In women, there were also significant increases in the rates of breast cancer (8%), colorectal cancer (8%), and malignant melanoma of the skin (by more than a third, 37%).
There were no cases of cervical cancer in women under 25 following the introduction of the HPV vaccine.
There were also significant decreases in the rates of lung cancer, cancer of unknown primary, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and kidney cancer.
  - Published5 hours ago
 ![Person sitting in a hospital room wearing a pink top, with a bandaged arm and medical dressing visible. The person holds a necklace while raising one finger. Hospital equipment, tubing, and a bed are visible in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/0e6f/live/a9a90390-9a3b-11f1-a86b-519b4d19bbee.jpg)
- ![A nurse provides assistance to a patient undergoing a mammogram in a medical facility.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/b530/live/270fa110-fb70-11f0-b7fd-f5e7f9ed0815.jpg)
- ![Sir Chris Hoy, wearing sunglasses and a blue top next to a woman in a dark jacket, also wearing sunglasses](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/926/cpsprodpb/a6a2/live/1b499b90-23a9-11f1-9a4e-e13728524fa3.jpg)
summary: Bowel cancer cases among people under 50 in Scotland have reached a record high, prompting the Scottish government to ask the UK National Screening Committee to consider lowering the screening age to 45. Public Health Scotland figures show that incidence in the under-50s has jumped by 38% over the past decade, with younger women experiencing a 56% increase. While no definitive cause has been identified, experts suggest factors like ultra-processed foods, microplastics, and lifestyle habits may be disrupting gut health.
key_points: Nearly 290 new bowel cancer cases were recorded in under-50s in Scotland in 2024, marking a 38% increase over the past decade.
Rates among younger women rose by 56%, compared to a 24% increase in younger men.
The Scottish government has requested that the UK National Screening Committee review lowering the routine screening age from 50 to 45.
Experts are investigating potential drivers for the rise, including ultra-processed foods, pesticides, microplastics, and forever chemicals that affect the gut microbiome.

title: One dead and hundreds ill in UK salmonella outbreak
author: Michelle Roberts
content:
One dead and hundreds ill in UK salmonella outbreak
![Getty Images A box of eggs](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/f3f2/live/595da390-9af5-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg.webp) Getty Images
A person has died and hundreds have fallen ill with salmonella food poisoning in an outbreak that UK experts believe is linked to eating food made with imported eggs.
More than a third of those affected - some babies and others as old as 90 - have needed hospital care, with two developing serious blood poisoning. Most people get better without treatment, however.
While salmonella cases can happen any time, this outbreak involves a specific, identical strain.
What are the symptoms?
Symptoms include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting or fever. These usually develop between 12 and 72 hours after becoming infected.
Anyone who is concerned should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance, says the UKHSA.
Most cases - 199 of the 207 - have been in England, including 47 in London and 38 in Yorkshire and Humber.
There have been six cases in Scotland, one in Wales and another in Northern Ireland.
Hannah Charles, lead epidemiologist for gastrointestinal infections at UKHSA, said: "We're working with Food Standards Agency and other public health agencies to investigate a salmonella outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK."
Salmonella can be found in a number of food sources including raw or under-cooked poultry or meat and eggs.
Preparing and cooking food thoroughly can prevent infection, as well as washing your hands after using the bathroom and before handling food.
Thousands of cases food poisoning happen each year in the UK caused by lots of different strains of salmonella.
It is more unusual to see an outbreak like this linked to one specific strain of the bacterium affecting many people at one time.
Experts say it is likely there could be more cases to come and some people may have been unwell but not reported it.
The UKHSA says "extensive" epidemiological and food chain investigations are ongoing to identify the source but that egg consumption remains the strongest to date.
People appear to have fallen ill after eating out rather than after consuming food prepared at home.
Some of the food businesses linked to 24 of the cases use imported eggs.
"At this time there is no identified link to UK-produced eggs or poultry," says the UKHSA.
Any extra precautions or preventative measures will be implemented if needed, it says. The risk to the general public is low.
Jacquelyn McCormick, Head of Incidents at the Food Standards Agency, said eggs which are thoroughly cooked and handled hygienically should not present a food safety risk.
She advised: "Infants, young children, pregnant people and older adults should only eat runny or raw eggs if they have a British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain egg assurance scheme."
People handling eggs, eggshells or egg packaging should wash their hands thoroughly with soap and water, she added.
![Alamy An egg with a British Lion mark on](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/4a6e/live/ef07ea30-9b23-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg.webp) Alamy
Catering outlets have a food hygiene rating, so looking at these when deciding where to eat, recommends Dr Kathleen O'Reilly from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.
Nick Allen, chief executive of the British Egg Industry Council, said hens in the UK had mandatory salmonella vaccinations, but "increasing volumes of imports" produced under "less stringent regulations" continue to arrive in Britain.
summary: A salmonella outbreak in the UK has resulted in one death and hundreds of illnesses, with experts linking the cases to imported eggs. Over a third of those affected required hospital care, and officials note that most victims fell ill after eating out. Extensive investigations are ongoing, though authorities emphasize that the overall risk to the general public remains low.
key_points: One person has died and hundreds have fallen ill in a UK salmonella outbreak linked to a specific strain of the bacterium.
More than a third of affected individuals required hospital care, with cases spanning England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
Investigations by the UKHSA and Food Standards Agency suggest a strong link to imported eggs used by food businesses.
Officials advise vulnerable groups to consume only eggs with specific British assurance schemes if they are runny or raw.
Thorough cooking and good hand hygiene can prevent salmonella infection, and there is currently no link to UK-produced eggs.

title: Rising number of people seeking ADHD diagnosis without treatment, say experts
author: Rachel Hall
content:
People are increasingly seeking to an obtain an ADHD diagnosis without pursuing treatment, according to experts who have called for more research to understand why.
Some people now regard ADHD as “an identity, rather than a disorder”, with the result that many obtain assessments from poor quality private providers, which lead them to “believe they have a condition needing treatment”, said the psychiatrist Dr Marios Adamou, the founder of the UK Adult ADHD Network.
This has resulted in a growth in complaints against NHS doctors when they are forced to reject low quality assessments, he added.
Adamou had seen recent figures showing that 50% of child patients did not pursue treatment after diagnosis, and observed a similar trend among adult patients in his clinic.
Some patients seek low, non-therapeutic doses of medication instead. “A lot of people would benefit from having amphetamines. You feel better, you can focus better, you can do more. But there hasn’t been a debate that this country should be cognitively augmented to increase productivity with stimulants,” he said.
“Why do people feel they can identify with these conditions? They are manifestations of a societal problem.”
Adamou was speaking ahead of a new Channel 4 documentary airing on 18 August titled The Great ADHD Myth?. It is presented by the NHS psychiatrist Dr Max Pemberton, who concludes that ADHD is a “social construct” rather than a medical condition, and that schools should adapt to better support a wider range of children rather than medicating them into fitting into a restrictive norm.
![Mother Shauna stands behind son Mason, her hands on his shoulders.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/428419d49712225c1ab892af5ae1ca0bb0a40f06/0_0_3354_4000/master/3354.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Adamou said that ADHD was both a social construct and a brain disorder. Brain differences are well established through research, and the diagnostic criteria has undergone “a lot of scientific scrutiny and validation”, he said, but added that in recent years “the ADHD concept has been expanded so much, it’s risking becoming meaningless … it’s socially constructed now, it’s something different than what it actually is.”
He said this phenomenon was fuelled by “challenges with the quality and the regulation of the [ADHD services] market”.
“Most of the assessment in the UK is now provided by the private sector,” he said. “I don’t think there’s any other medical condition where the private sector provides as much care … When you have private providers providing the majority of care in a market system with a diagnosis that is commoditised, and attracts stimulants, you may have issues.”
Despite this, he stressed that there was thought to be underdiagnosis of ADHD. Poor quality diagnoses have created “a double stigma” for many people with the condition. “Not only do you have stigma because you have ADHD, but also there’s stigma about whether you have real ADHD,” he said.
Prof Dinesh Bhugra, the former head of the Royal College of Psychiatrists who features in the documentary, agreed that “there has certainly been a splurge of diagnosis, and we don’t know why that is”.
He said: “The question is why now, and why this? What is it providing? My fear is we medicalise normal human responses because it gives us the power as clinicians and it gives people the label which allows them to either feel they’ve got certain privileges or it gives them certain cachet in society.”
In the documentary, he shares his concerns about the growing role of profiteering private companies supplying services that the NHS is under too much strain to provide. ADHD assessment was “an easy way to make money” for private companies, he said, adding: “Their responsibility is to the shareholders, not the general public.”
Bhugra feared that the UK’s current approach was an American import, where the DSM [Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders]’s checklist-style approach to assessment reflected the demands of insurance companies, and a culture of “health is a commodity and you can buy it and sell it”.
He agreed with the documentary’s message that services should be reformed to take a more holistic approach, bringing together the social, biological and psychological facts of ADHD rather than emphasising medical intervention.
Jessica Lister, a clinical director and consultant nurse at the private provider Care ADHD, feared that the documentary’s message could be harmful. “Dismissing ADHD as a social construct doesn’t just trivialise an established clinical condition – it perpetuates the inequalities faced by people with ADHD across education, health, employment and the justice system,” she said.
“The question here isn’t whether ADHD is a real medical problem – it’s whether systems respond early enough, consistently enough and fairly enough to prevent avoidable harm … The real problems are long waits, inequitable access, inconsistent quality and too little joined-up support across health, education, care and employment.”
Mark Pattison, the chief executive of Care ADHD, said that it was important to differentiate between private providers, adding that his organisation’s clinical governance was as strong as the NHS ADHD and mental health services he had run for 15 years. “Profit should never come before clinical quality. But efficiency isn’t the enemy of it either,” he said.
He added: “Standards need to apply to everyone, not just us. Some NHS trusts have children waiting two, five, even 10 years for an assessment. That’s not safe care, whoever provides it. Some private providers fall short too.”
The Great ADHD Myth? is available to watch and stream on Channel 4 at 8pm, Tuesday 18 August.
summary: Experts report a rising number of individuals seeking ADHD diagnoses without pursuing treatment, often viewing the condition as an identity rather than a disorder. This trend is linked by some to poor-quality private providers, a commoditised diagnostic market, and the medicalisation of normal human responses. While critics argue ADHD is becoming a meaningless social construct, other clinical professionals warn that dismissing the condition trivializes a real medical issue and worsens existing inequalities.
key_points: Experts have observed a growing trend of adults and children obtaining ADHD diagnoses without following through with treatment.
Concerns have been raised regarding poor-quality private providers and a commoditised market system that issues low-quality assessments.
A forthcoming Channel 4 documentary features psychiatrists debating whether ADHD is a medical condition or a social construct.
Some clinicians fear that normal human responses are being medicalized, creating a double stigma for individuals with genuine ADHD.
Representatives from private providers caution that dismissing ADHD as a social construct perpetuates inequalities and ignores systemic failings like long NHS wait times.

title: Scrapping men’s right to prostate cancer tests ‘will cost lives’
author: Michael Searles
content:
The decision to strip men of the right to a prostate cancer test “will cost lives”, a leading expert has warned.
The Telegraph revealed last week that men aged over 50 are no longer entitled to a blood test to help identify the disease, with GPs instead deciding who is given one.
The decision to remove men’s right to have a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test has been condemned by politicians, celebrities and now doctors.
Prof Chris Booth, an expert member of the EU prostate cancer screening programme’s scientific advisory board, criticised the Government’s “surreptitious” decision to withdraw the decades-old guidance.
The former urological surgeon and founder of Chaps, a men’s health charity, said the UK already had higher death rates from prostate cancer than other Western countries and that the decision would make it worse.
In a letter to the The Telegraph, Prof Booth said: “This latest manoeuvre by the DHSC will do nothing to improve the service and will almost certainly cost lives.”
summary: A leading medical expert has warned that a government decision to remove men's automatic right to a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test will cost lives. Under the new guidance, men over 50 are no longer entitled to the blood test, with GPs now deciding who receives one. This withdrawal of decades-old guidance has been condemned by doctors, politicians, and celebrities.
key_points: Men over 50 are no longer entitled to a routine prostate cancer blood test.
GPs will now decide which patients are given a PSA test.
Prof Chris Booth warned that the decision will worsen the UK's high prostate cancer death rates.
The decision to withdraw the decades-old guidance was criticized as surreptitious.

title: Brits say ‘why have I got lurgy in summer’ as nation hit by wave of illness - AOL
author: Ben Hurst
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![People in the UK are complaining of a wave of sickness like colds or flu - or even Covid - this summer](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/18/4c2195c6-f3c3-3123-9857-83f608f277bd/e2b63cea-fe4e-4c92-ab13-bb531f941d37.jpg)
People are complaining that a ‘summer lurgy’ is sweeping the UK - and fear there’s been a summer surge of Covid. People have taken to social media to complain of coughs, sniffles, sore throats and headaches - and wonder how it can happen in a heatwave.
Google Trends has reported that over the past week, “can you get the flu in summer?” is a ‘breakout’ term, signifying a growth of over 5,000% in search interest. The NHS is under pressure this summer with high attendances in A&E caused probably by the weather which has brought an increase in existing conditions worsening.
During the May and June 2026 heat events the UK Health Security Agency reported an estimated total of 2,877 heat-associated deaths - already near the highest levels ever recorded for a whole year. Respiratory conditions are known to be worstened by the heat.
Heatwaves also cause people to be more exposed as air conditioning and staying indoors to get out the heat can caused increase spreading.
In California and America reports suggest the summer peak of Covid-19 is in fact higher now than the winter. Dr. Erica Pan, director of the California Department of Public Health said: ““Anyone who hasn’t received a 2025-26 dose, or is due for the second dose, is encouraged to get vaccinated now, before the next COVID-19 surge,”
“Disease is on the rise in California, where we’re seeing increasing cases, increasing test positivity, increasing in our wastewater. This is a good time, actually, to protect yourselves or your family,” Pan told The Times in an interview, “because we anticipate, based on the last couple of years at least, that this may be the larger peak than the winter.”
On social media people complained at the cold surge. One said: ”I have that ‘summer flu’ that everybody’s going on about and I can confirm that it’s definitely Covid.” Another added: “how does someone get nasopharyngitis in the summer? how is this even possible!! i’m dying from the heat and now i have to deal with this inflammation and the flu?"
One speculated: “I’m suspecting we’re in the midst of a summer surge. A suspicious number of colleagues had headaches that went on for days. I’m getting over a ear infection and a relative has shingles.”
Frosty said: “I’m sick of having the flu in the middle of summer lol”. River added: “Currently under the weather and praying I don’t have the flu …. Summer sickness is the absolute worst! Have a good night folks it’s cold meds and sleep for me.”
A Londoner posted on social media: “Me and all my friends have gotten individually ill in the last week. Seems there is some gross summer cold travelling around at the moment. Haven’t left the house since last weekend, and seems my cold is just getting worse by each day!
“Feeling very sorry for myself, the heat is not helping, both in the sense of it’s too hot to be ill, and can’t go out in the cool mornings.”
Another added: “My team at work has had it this week, passed on at an event we attended.” Another person said: “Yes!!! Took out my entire family for a week!”
Dr Dominic Greenyer, a private doctor at the Health Suite, said: “Throughout the year, there are multiple viruses that come and go, and often, there can be clusters. So certain viruses may cause a cluster of cases, which we may be seeing at the moment in London. COVID is one of many viruses that circulate through the natural population every year.
“With these viruses, you can’t tell initially what it is because there’s a lot of crossover with symptoms. Most viruses cause symptoms such as muscle aches, high temperatures, and fever; these are just symptoms of feeling unwell. It’s hard to pin down a particular virus without getting tested but as most patients get better with no treatment, they don’t get tested. It’s usually only the patients who are very unwell and are admitted to the hospital who get tested.
“In 2020, we had a particularly severe strain that obviously caused a lot of health problems across the nation. However, is there something specific we should worry about with summer colds? No, not specifically. It could be viruses like COVID, among other things.
“General medical advice would be good self-care, get plenty of rest, fluids, a balanced diet, because all these things help the body to heal, regardless of what the cause is.”
Dr Greenyer also noted that most people tend to get better within 10-14 days and require ‘no intervention from medical services’. A pharmacist can give treatment advice and recommend flu remedies.
The NHS is urging millions of people to book their flu jab from today as the health service starts winter preparations earlier than ever.
As of yesterday (August 17), the national booking system is open so eligible people, including pregnant women and children, can pre-book their flu vaccinations when vaccinations start on September 1.
The NHS said it wants to do everything it can to ease winter demand after back-to-back heatwaves have seen staff treat record numbers this summer.
A&E attendances hit a record 2.5 million attendances in July – and staff experienced the 3 busiest months ever recorded between May and July in emergency departments.
Despite the record pressure, more patients were seen, treated or discharged within 4 hours than in June, with performance improving to 75.4%.
Flu season usually peaks in December and January, so the NHS is starting vaccinations in autumn, to ensure those at risk are protected and fewer people are hospitalised.
summary: People across the UK are complaining of a summer wave of illness, including colds, flu-like symptoms, and suspected Covid-19 during recent heatwaves. Google Trends reported a massive spike in searches regarding summer flu, while the NHS has faced high A&E attendances due to worsening conditions and summer weather. Health experts note that multiple circulating viruses can cause overlapping symptoms, and the NHS has responded by launching early flu jab bookings to ease future demand.
key_points: A wave of summer illness featuring coughs, sniffles, and headaches is affecting people across the UK.
Google Trends noted a 5,000% increase in search interest for 'can you get the flu in summer?' over a single week.
The UK Health Security Agency reported 2,877 heat-associated deaths during May and June 2026 heat events, placing heavy pressure on NHS emergency departments.
Medical experts advise that multiple circulating viruses share similar symptoms and that most people recover with self-care and rest within 10 to 14 days.
The NHS has opened its national booking system early for autumn flu vaccinations to help reduce winter demand.

title: Babies born under sugar rationing grew into adults with lower cancer risk
author: Weilong Zhang
content:
Could how much sugar you consumed before your second birthday shape your health decades later – even into your 70s?
A new study that my colleagues and I conducted suggests the answer could be yes. People who had less sugar exposure during the first few years of life were much less likely to develop several different cancers later in life, and they also showed signs of slower biological ageing. We also found that even in adulthood, they continued to consume less sugar and had healthier diets overall.
This is not an easy question to study in real life. Researchers obviously can’t run that experiment on real babies – split them into groups, feed one group sugar, then wait 70 years to see what happens.
Britain’s postwar sugar rationing offered a rare alternative. After the second world war, sugar remained rationed in Britain for several years. But in September 1953, rationing ended and people started eating a lot more sugar. Consumption nearly doubled. This meant that children born just a few months apart had very different levels of sugar exposure both in the womb and during early childhood.
For our study, we used data from over 64,000 people born in Britain between 1951 and 1956. Those born earlier spent a larger share of their first 1,000 days under sugar rationing, while those born later experienced progressively less of it.
By the first 1,000 days, we mean the period from conception to a child’s second birthday. This is a critical stage because the body is developing very rapidly. Organs are growing, metabolism is taking shape, and the immune system is maturing.
Food and taste preferences also begin to form during this period. Although 1,000 days is a relatively short period, the effects of the food environment during this stage can last throughout a person’s life.
To track cancer cases, we used the UK Biobank – a huge health database that follows participants for decades and records, among other things, who develops cancer and when.
We found that people who experienced longer periods of sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days had a lower incidence of five types of cancer: breast, prostate, liver, rectal and lung cancer. The effect was strongest for liver cancer, where rates were around 69% lower, and weakest – though still substantial – for breast cancer, at 36% lower. Importantly, these differences only began to appear decades after sugar rationing had ended.
We also found that exposure to sugar rationing is related to biological ageing. Biological age is not the same as chronological age. Two people may both be 70 years old, while their cells and immune systems show different levels of ageing.
One way we measure biological ageing is through telomere length. Telomeres are protective structures located at the ends of chromosomes. As cells age, telomeres usually become shorter.
We found that people who experienced longer periods of sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days had longer telomeres. Based on our estimates, this difference is equivalent to about 2.2 years of slower biological ageing.
We also found lower levels of a protein called granzyme B, which rises when the immune system has been working overtime for years – another sign of slower ageing at a cellular level. Taken together, these results suggest that lower sugar exposure early in life may be related to slower ageing at the cellular level.
The sugar habit that lasted 50 years
What is most surprising, however, is not the cancer results or the biological markers of ageing. It’s how early-life sugar exposure continued to affect people’s diets even 50 years later.
We found that people who experienced sugar rationing early in life still consumed less sugar in adulthood, around age 50. They also ate less overall, and their diets were healthier and more diverse. This suggests that the level of sweetness people are exposed to very early in life may shape their taste preferences for a long time.
There appear to be two mechanisms at work. One is biological – early nutrition may shape how the metabolism, organs and immune system develop. The other is behavioural – a taste for less sweetness, formed early, seems to stick.
Other research using the end of Britain’s sugar rationing has also found that people who experienced more sugar rationing early in life had lower risks of type 2 diabetes and hypertension. A recent study using the same end of Britain’s sugar rationing found lower risks of dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, while another study reported lower risks of heart disease and stroke.
This does not mean that children should not eat sugar at all, and it certainly does not mean that postwar sugar rationing is a desirable policy. What this historical evidence shows is that, during a critical period of development, even relatively small differences in sugar exposure over a short period may leave effects that are still observable half a century later.
Children may not remember what they ate before age two. But their later health, their bodies and even their taste preferences may still carry the imprint of those very early-life experiences.
summary: A new study analyzing data from over 64,000 people born in Britain during postwar sugar rationing found that individuals exposed to less sugar during their first 1,000 days had a lower risk of several cancers, showed signs of slower biological aging, and maintained healthier diets in adulthood. The research leverages the end of sugar rationing in September 1953, which caused sugar consumption to nearly double and created distinct differences in early childhood sugar exposure. These findings indicate that early-life nutrition significantly impacts long-term health outcomes, biological aging, and lifelong taste preferences.
key_points: People who experienced longer periods of sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days had a lower incidence of breast, prostate, liver, rectal, and lung cancers later in life.
Individuals exposed to early-life sugar rationing exhibited longer telomeres and lower levels of granzyme B, indicating slower cellular aging.
Those who had less early-life sugar consumption maintained healthier, more diverse diets and consumed less sugar overall even at age 50.
The first 1,000 days from conception to age two represent a critical developmental window where diet shapes long-term metabolism, immunity, and taste preferences.

title: One dead and hundreds ill in UK salmonella outbreak
author: Michelle Roberts
content:
![A box of eggs](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/f3f2/live/595da390-9af5-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
- Published
A person has died and hundreds have fallen ill with salmonella food posioning in an outbreak that UK experts believe is linked to eating food made with imported eggs.
The UK Health Security Agency has launched an investigation, external into the 207 cases it has seen in the past year, with most recorded in recent weeks.
More than a third of those affected - some babies and others as old as 90 - have needed hospital care, with two developing serious blood poisoning. Most people get better without treatment, however.
While salmonella cases can happen any time, this outbreak involves a specific, identical strain.
Diarrhoea and vomiting
Symptoms include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting or fever. These usually develop between 12 and 72 hours after becoming infected.
Anyone who is concerned should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance, says the UKHSA.
Most cases - 199 of the 207 - have been in England, including 47 in London and 38 in Yorkshire and Humber.
Hannah Charles, lead epidemiologist for gastrointestinal infections at UKHSA, said: "We're working with Food Standards Agency and other public health agencies to investigate a salmonella outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK."
Salmonella can be found in a number of food sources including raw or under-cooked poultry or meat and eggs.
Preparing and cooking food thoroughly can prevent infection, as well as washing your hands after using the bathroom and before handling food.
Thousands of cases food poisoning happen each year in the UK caused by lots of different strains of salmonella.
It is more unusual to see an outbreak like this linked to one specific stain of the bacterium affecting many people at one time.
The UKHSA says "extensive" epidemiological and food chain investigations are ongoing to identify the source but that egg consumption remains the strongest to date.
Some of the food businesses linked to 24 of the cases use imported eggs.
"At this time there is no identified link to UK-produced eggs or poultry," says the UKHSA.
Any extra precautions or preventative measures will be implemented if needed, it says. The risk to the general public is low.
Jacquelyn McCormick, Head of Incidents at the Food Standards Agency, said eggs which are thoroughly cooked and handled hygienically should not present a food safety risk.
She advised: "Infants, young children, pregnant people and older adults should only eat runny or raw eggs if they have a British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain egg assurance scheme."
People handling eggs, eggshells or egg packaging should wash their hands thoroughly with soap and water, she added.
summary: A salmonella outbreak in the UK has resulted in one death and 207 recorded cases over the past year, with experts linking the infections to imported eggs. Over a third of those affected have required hospital care, though the overall risk to the general public remains low. Authorities are continuing extensive investigations, while advising thorough cooking and proper hygiene.
key_points: One person has died and 207 cases have been linked to a specific strain of salmonella in the UK.
Investigators believe the outbreak is connected to food made with imported eggs rather than UK-produced eggs.
More than a third of affected individuals, ranging from babies to 90-year-olds, required hospital treatment.
Symptoms include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting, and fever, typically appearing 12 to 72 hours after infection.
Vulnerable groups are advised to consume runny or raw eggs only if they carry the British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain scheme.
